description: Hypotheses, variables and the four sampling methods: random, opportunity, systematic, stratified.
content_html:
The Starting Point of Scientific Research

Every psychological study starts with a question. A researcher notices something about human behaviour and wants to know why it happens, or whether one thing influences another. But noticing something and testing it scientifically are very different tasks. Before any data can be collected, a researcher must be precise: they must state exactly what they expect to find, define what they are measuring and ensure they have an appropriate group of participants. These steps are the foundation of scientific psychology.

Hypotheses

A hypothesis is a precise, testable prediction. It states in advance what the researcher expects to find. A hypothesis must be operationalised — meaning both the independent variable and the dependent variable must be defined in terms of how they will be measured, not described vaguely.

Compare these two predictions: “People who revise more will do better” versus “Participants who revise using flashcards for five hours will recall more words from a 20-word list than participants who reread their notes for five hours.” The second is a well-operationalised hypothesis because both conditions of the independent variable (flashcards vs rereading) and the dependent variable (words recalled from a 20-word list) are clearly defined and measurable.

Key Fact

A well-operationalised hypothesis states both conditions of the independent variable AND a clearly measurable dependent variable. Without operationalisation, a hypothesis cannot be properly tested, and mark schemes require both elements for full marks.

Null and Alternative Hypotheses

Every study involves two complementary hypotheses. The null hypothesis states that there is no difference or no relationship between the variables — any result found is due to chance. For example: “There will be no significant difference in word recall between participants who revise with flashcards and those who reread notes.”

The alternative hypothesis (also called the experimental hypothesis) states that there will be a difference or relationship — this is what the researcher expects to find. For example: “Participants who revise using flashcards will recall significantly more words from a 20-word list than those who reread their notes.”

Statistical testing after the study will determine whether the data allows the null hypothesis to be rejected. If results are ‘significant’ (unlikely to be due to chance), the null hypothesis is rejected and the alternative hypothesis is supported. Psychologists do not ‘prove’ their hypotheses; they provide evidence for or against them.

A independent variable (IV) is the one the researcher changes or manipulates. In the flashcard example, the IV is the revision method (flashcards vs rereading).

A dependent variable (DV) is what the researcher measures — the outcome. In the flashcard example, the DV is the number of words recalled from the 20-word list.

Extraneous variables are any other variables that could affect the DV that the researcher has not controlled. For example, if one group of participants had a higher baseline memory ability, that could explain any difference in word recall rather than the revision method. Controlling extraneous variables is essential to ensure results reflect the IV rather than something else.

Target Populations and Samples

A researcher almost never studies every member of a group they are interested in. Instead, they select a sample from the target population. The sample should be representative — it should reflect the characteristics of the target population as closely as possible so that conclusions can be generalised beyond the study itself.

Random sampling gives every member of the target population an equal chance of being selected. The researcher lists all members of the population and uses a random process (lottery, random number generator) to select participants. Strength: unbiased and representative. Weakness: requires a complete list of the population, which is often difficult to obtain, and non-responders may create a biased final sample.

Opportunity sampling selects whoever is available and willing to take part. A researcher standing at a university entrance and asking passers-by is using opportunity sampling. Strength: quick, easy and inexpensive. Weakness: biased towards people who are easily available at that time and place, so the sample may not be representative of the target population.

Systematic sampling selects every nth person from a list. For example, if there are 1,000 people in the population and you need 100 participants, you would select every 10th person. Strength: straightforward to carry out and reduces researcher bias. Weakness: may still be biased if the list has a pattern that makes every nth person systematically different.

Stratified sampling divides the population into subgroups (strata) based on relevant characteristics (e.g. age, gender) and then randomly selects participants from each stratum in proportion to their size in the full population. Strength: ensures the sample reflects the population structure, making it highly representative. Weakness: time-consuming and requires detailed knowledge of the population’s structure.

Key Fact

Four sampling methods: random (equal chance, unbiased but hard to obtain full list), opportunity (quick but biased towards available people), systematic (every nth person, straightforward but potential pattern bias), stratified (proportional subgroups, highly representative but time-consuming).
exam_tip_html: Hypothesis questions are very commonly misanswered. A hypothesis must have both conditions of the IV AND a measurable DV — if either is missing or vague, you will not get full marks. Always check: does my hypothesis say exactly what both groups are doing differently? Does it say exactly what is being measured? For sampling method questions, state the method, describe briefly how it works, then give one specific strength and one specific weakness — do not just name the method.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The null hypothesis predicts no difference (any result is due to chance); the alternative hypothesis predicts a difference or relationship. Both must be operationalised with clearly defined IV conditions and a measurable DV.
  • The IV is what the researcher manipulates; the DV is what is measured; extraneous variables are other factors that must be controlled to ensure the results reflect the IV.
  • Four sampling methods: random (unbiased but needs full list), opportunity (easy but biased), systematic (every nth person, straightforward), stratified (proportional subgroups, most representative).

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a correctly operationalised hypothesis?
A) People who sleep more will feel better
B) Students who get more sleep will have higher exam scores
C) Participants who sleep for 8 hours will score higher on a 20-item memory test than participants who sleep for 4 hours
D) Sleep affects memory
practice_questions.marks: C) Participants who sleep for 8 hours will score higher on a 20-item memory test than participants who sleep for 4 hours [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define what is meant by an 'extraneous variable'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'Any variable, other than the IV, that could affect the DV and therefore reduce the validity of the study.' — both elements present and clearly linked.
Secure: Core idea correct — names variable other than IV and mentions DV or validity.
Developing: Vague — mentions something affecting results without reference to IV or DV.
Emerging: Incorrect or incomplete definition.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a researcher could use stratified sampling to select participants for a study.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- Divide the target population into subgroups (strata) based on relevant characteristics (e.g. age, gender, year group).
- Calculate the proportion each subgroup represents in the full population.
- Randomly select participants from each subgroup in proportion to its size.
Mastering: All three steps described clearly.
Secure: Two steps with correct terminology.
Developing: General idea of subgroups without proportionality.
Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: A researcher wants to study whether background music affects reading comprehension. Write a suitable alternative (experimental) hypothesis for this study.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should:
- State a directional or non-directional prediction.
- Operationalise the IV (e.g. two conditions: music vs no music, or specific type of music vs silence).
- Operationalise the DV (e.g. score on a 10-question comprehension test based on a given passage).
- Example: 'Participants who read a passage with background music playing will score lower on a 10-question comprehension test than participants who read in silence.'
Mastering: Both IV conditions and DV clearly operationalised, directional or non-directional stated.
Secure: IV and DV present, one not fully operationalised.
Developing: IV or DV missing.
Emerging: Vague prediction only.

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between a null hypothesis and an alternative hypothesis.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should cover:
- Null hypothesis: predicts no significant difference or relationship between variables; any result is due to chance.
- Alternative hypothesis: predicts there will be a difference or relationship; what the researcher expects.
- Both require operationalisation (both conditions of IV and measurable DV).
- After statistical testing: if results are significant, the null hypothesis is rejected and the alternative is supported.
- Psychologists support or reject hypotheses based on evidence; they do not 'prove' them.
Mastering: All five elements clearly and accurately described.
Secure: Four elements present.
Developing: Null and alternative distinguished, one or two additional points.
Emerging: Basic distinction only.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the four main sampling methods used in psychological research.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1):
- Random: every member of population has equal chance; uses lottery or random numbers.
- Opportunity: selects whoever is available and willing.
- Systematic: selects every nth person from a list.
- Stratified: divides population into subgroups, selects proportionally from each.

Evaluation (AO3):
- Random: strength — unbiased and representative if done correctly. Weakness — requires full list; non-response bias.
- Opportunity: strength — quick, cheap, easy. Weakness — biased towards available groups; not representative.
- Systematic: strength — avoids researcher bias, straightforward. Weakness — may have pattern bias if list is structured.
- Stratified: strength — most representative method; reflects population structure. Weakness — time-consuming; requires detailed knowledge of population.
- Overall: stratified produces the most representative sample but opportunity is most commonly used due to practicality.

Mastering: All four methods described correctly, with elaborated strengths and weaknesses.
Secure: Three methods described well with evaluation.
Developing: Two methods described, some evaluation.
Emerging: One or two methods, limited evaluation.

knowledge_checks.q: Which sampling method selects every nth person from a list of the target population?
The null hypothesis predicts that any difference found between conditions will be due to:
The variable that the researcher deliberately changes or manipulates is called the _____ variable.
A hypothesis must be _____, meaning both the IV conditions and the DV must be clearly defined and measurable.
Match each sampling method to its key feature:
right: Every member has an equal chance of selection
Selects whoever is available at the time

flashcard_questions.a: A testable, precise prediction about the relationship between variables, stated before a study.

flashcard_questions.q: What does it mean to operationalise a hypothesis?
flashcard_questions.a: To define both IV conditions and the DV in measurable, specific terms.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the null hypothesis predict?
flashcard_questions.a: No significant difference or relationship between variables — any difference is due to chance.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the alternative hypothesis predict?
flashcard_questions.a: That there will be a significant difference or relationship between variables.
The variable the researcher deliberately changes or manipulates.
The variable the researcher measures as the outcome of the study.
Any variable other than the IV that could affect the DV and reduce validity.
Every member of the target population has an equal chance of being selected.

flashcard_questions.q: What is one weakness of opportunity sampling?
flashcard_questions.a: It is biased towards people who are conveniently available, so may not represent the population.
Dividing the population into subgroups and selecting participants in proportion from each.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is stratified sampling considered the most representative method?
flashcard_questions.a: Because it reflects the actual structure of the target population across relevant subgroups.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the target population in psychological research?
flashcard_questions.a: The entire group a researcher wants to draw conclusions about.

glossary_terms.definition: A testable, precise prediction about the relationship between two variables, stated before a study is conducted.
The process of clearly defining a variable in a way that can be measured, for example defining 'stress' as a score on a validated stress questionnaire.
A prediction that there is no difference or no relationship between the variables being studied, and that any difference found is due to chance.
A prediction that states there will be a difference or relationship between variables; it is what the researcher expects to find.
The variable that the researcher deliberately changes or manipulates to see if it causes a change in the dependent variable.
The variable that is measured by the researcher; it is expected to change as a result of the independent variable.
Any variable other than the independent variable that could affect the dependent variable, potentially reducing the validity of the study.
A subset of the target population selected to take part in a study, used to represent the larger group.
The entire group that a researcher wants to draw conclusions about, from which a sample is drawn.
A sampling method in which every member of the target population has an equal chance of being selected, for example using a lottery or random number generator.
A sampling method in which participants are selected from whoever is available and willing to take part at the time of the study.
A sampling method in which every nth member of the target population is selected, for example every tenth person on a list.
A sampling method in which the population is divided into subgroups and participants are selected from each subgroup in proportion to their representation in the population.

hero_image_caption: Careful research design begins with a precise hypothesis and representative sample.
